title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Overview, Etiology, and Management
chunk_text: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Overview, Etiology, and Management. Disease: Type 2 Diabetes. Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia resulting from impaired insulin secretion and peripheral insulin resistance. Over time, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes leads to microvascular complications including diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and peripheral neuropathy, as well as macrovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Regular glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) monitoring, blood pressure control, and lipid management are crucial pillars of clinical care. Patient education on self-monitoring of blood glucose and foot care prevents severe secondary morbidity.

title: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Autoimmune Pathophysiology and Insulin Therapy
chunk_text: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Autoimmune Pathophysiology and Insulin Therapy. Disease: Type 1 Diabetes. Type 1 diabetes mellitus is an autoimmune endocrine disorder typically presenting in childhood or early adulthood, although onset can occur at any age. The destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells leads to absolute insulin deficiency. Without exogenous insulin replacement, patients rapidly develop diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening medical emergency marked by ketone accumulation, metabolic acidosis, and severe dehydration. Intensive insulin therapy matching insulin doses to carbohydrate intake and physical exertion is essential to maintain target glycemic levels and minimize hypoglycemia.

title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Maternal-Fetal Considerations and Screening
chunk_text: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Maternal-Fetal Considerations and Screening. Disease: Gestational Diabetes. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is defined as glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy, typically evaluated between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation using oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT). Uncontrolled maternal hyperglycemia increases the risk of macrosomia, birth trauma, neonatal hypoglycemia, respiratory distress syndrome, and preeclampsia. Postpartum follow-up is essential as women with gestational diabetes have a significantly elevated lifetime risk of developing chronic type 2 diabetes mellitus.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Recognition, Biochemical Mechanisms, and Emergency Protocol
chunk_text: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Recognition, Biochemical Mechanisms, and Emergency Protocol. Disease: Diabetic Ketoacidosis. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute, critical metabolic complication seen primarily in type 1 diabetes but also occurring in type 2 diabetes during severe physiologic stress. Lack of insulin prevents cellular glucose utilization, driving the breakdown of adipose tissue into free fatty acids which are converted by the liver into acidic ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate). This produces severe anion-gap metabolic acidosis and osmotic diuresis leading to profound fluid and electrolyte depletion requiring intensive hemodynamic monitoring.

chunk_text: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Recognition, Biochemical Mechanisms, and Emergency Protocol (Diabetic Ketoacidosis). Symptoms and Signs: Deep rapid breathing (Kussmaul respiration), acetone fruity breath odor, nausea, severe vomiting, abdominal pain, extreme dehydration, confusion, lethargy, stupor. Causes and Etiology: Profound insulin deficiency coupled with counter-regulatory hormone excess (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol), precipitating lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis. Common triggers include infection, missed insulin doses, or newly diagnosed diabetes.

title: Hypoglycemia in Diabetic Patients: Pathophysiology and Emergency Action
chunk_text: Hypoglycemia in Diabetic Patients: Pathophysiology and Emergency Action. Disease: Hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia is defined clinically as a plasma glucose concentration below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). It triggers autonomic activation resulting in neurogenic symptoms (shakiness, diaphoresis, palpitations) followed by neuroglycopenic manifestations (cognitive impairment, confusion, syncope) as cerebral glucose deprivation ensues. Severe hypoglycemia is a medical emergency that can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias, irreversible neurological injury, or death if not promptly reversed.

title: Essential Primary Hypertension: Pathogenesis and Clinical Guidelines
chunk_text: Essential Primary Hypertension: Pathogenesis and Clinical Guidelines. Disease: Primary Hypertension. Essential hypertension accounts for over 90% of all clinical hypertension cases and is diagnosed when systolic blood pressure is persistently >=130 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure >=80 mmHg. Chronic sustained hemodynamic strain accelerates atherosclerosis and causes left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, ischemic heart disease, and cerebrovascular accidents. Routine ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and patient adherence to long-term antihypertensive therapy are crucial to prevent irreversible target-organ damage.

title: Secondary Hypertension: Identifiable Causes and Diagnostic Workup
source: NIH MedlinePlus & European Society of Cardiology
chunk_text: Secondary Hypertension: Identifiable Causes and Diagnostic Workup. Disease: Secondary Hypertension. Secondary hypertension represents approximately 5-10% of adult hypertension cases where an identifiable, potentially curable cause exists. Suspecting secondary hypertension is indicated in patients with resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on three concurrent antihypertensives including a diuretic), severe sudden blood pressure surges, or abnormal clinical signs such as abdominal bruits or severe hypokalemia. Comprehensive diagnostic evaluation includes renal duplex ultrasonography, plasma renin-to-aldosterone ratio, overnight polysomnography, and plasma metanephrines.

title: Hypertensive Crisis: Hypertensive Urgency versus Hypertensive Emergency
chunk_text: Hypertensive Crisis: Hypertensive Urgency versus Hypertensive Emergency. Disease: Hypertensive Crisis. A hypertensive crisis is characterized by a severe elevation in blood pressure, typically systolic >180 mmHg and/or diastolic >120 mmHg. It is classified into two distinct clinical categories: hypertensive emergency, which involves acute, life-threatening target-organ damage (acute coronary syndrome, encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute renal failure, pulmonary edema), versus hypertensive urgency, where blood pressure is markedly elevated without acute organ impairment. Rapid uncontrolled lowering in urgency is contraindicated to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion.

title: Coronary Artery Disease: Atherosclerotic Plaque and Myocardial Ischemia
chunk_text: Coronary Artery Disease: Atherosclerotic Plaque and Myocardial Ischemia. Disease: Coronary Artery Disease. Coronary artery disease (CAD) develops as fibrofatty plaques progressively narrow coronary arterial lumens, limiting oxygen delivery to the myocardium during heightened metabolic demand. Stable angina manifests as predictable exertional pain relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Plaque rupture or erosion triggers acute platelet aggregation and thrombus formation, culminating in acute coronary syndromes (unstable angina or myocardial infarction). Coronary computed tomography angiography and invasive cardiac catheterization serve as gold-standard diagnostic tools.

title: Congestive Heart Failure: Systolic and Diastolic Ventricular Dysfunction
chunk_text: Congestive Heart Failure: Systolic and Diastolic Ventricular Dysfunction. Disease: Heart Failure. Congestive heart failure (CHF) is a complex clinical syndrome resulting from structural or functional cardiac impairment that prevents the ventricles from filling or ejecting blood effectively. It is categorized into heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Elevated intracardiac filling pressures result in pulmonary congestion and systemic venous hypertension. Serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or NT-proBNP measurement combined with transthoracic echocardiography is foundational for diagnosis and therapeutic staging.

title: Bronchial Asthma: Airway Hyperresponsiveness and Chronic Inflammation
source: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) & NIH MedlinePlus
chunk_text: Bronchial Asthma: Airway Hyperresponsiveness and Chronic Inflammation. Disease: Asthma. Bronchial asthma is a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory respiratory disease characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction, bronchial wall edema, and mucus hypersecretion. Spirometry demonstrates airflow limitation with significant reversibility following inhaled bronchodilator administration (increase in FEV1 >=12% and >=200 mL). Asthma phenotypes include allergic (atopic) asthma, non-allergic asthma, adult-onset asthma, and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Proper inhaler technique and adherence to daily anti-inflammatory controller therapy are essential to prevent severe exacerbations and airway remodeling.

chunk_text: The Common Cold: Rhinovirus Pathogenesis and Symptomatic Relief. Disease: Common Cold. The common cold is a self-limiting acute viral upper respiratory tract infection. Transmission occurs primarily through respiratory droplets and direct contact with fomites. Viral attachment to ICAM-1 receptors on nasopharyngeal epithelial cells triggers host chemokine release, leading to vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability, and glandular secretion. Symptoms typically peak within 2 to 3 days and resolve spontaneously within 7 to 10 days. Routine antibiotic administration is contraindicated as it confers no therapeutic benefit and drives antimicrobial resistance.

title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Transmission and DOTS Strategy
chunk_text: Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Transmission and DOTS Strategy. Disease: Tuberculosis. Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the world's deadliest infectious killers. Inhaled mycobacteria are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, initiating granuloma (tubercle) formation with caseous necrosis. In immunocompetent hosts, cell-mediated immunity contains the bacilli in a latent state; however, immunosuppression (especially HIV infection, malnutrition, or anti-TNF therapy) permits reactivation into active pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is confirmed by sputum smear microscopy for acid-fast bacilli, rapid molecular assays (GeneXpert MTB/RIF), and mycobacterial liquid culture.

chunk_text: Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB): Molecular Detection and Second-Line Regimens. Disease: Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis. chunk_text: COVID-19 Acute Respiratory Infection: SARS-CoV-2 Pathogenesis, Variants, and Antivirals. Disease: COVID-19. title: Tension-Type Headache: Diagnosis, Pericranial Tenderness, and Analgesic Stewardship
chunk_text: Tension-Type Headache: Diagnosis, Pericranial Tenderness, and Analgesic Stewardship. Disease: Tension Headache. Tension-type headache (TTH) is the most prevalent headache disorder globally. Unlike migraine, it is typically bilateral, non-throbbing, does not worsen with routine physical activity, and is not accompanied by nausea or vomiting. Chronic tension-type headache occurs >=15 days per month for >3 months and significantly impairs daily function. Overusing simple analgesics (>15 days/month) or combination analgesics (>10 days/month) risks inducing medication-overuse headache (rebound headache), which requires medication weaning and bridge therapy.

chunk_text: Iron Deficiency Anemia: Microcytic Hypochromic Erythropoiesis and Oral Iron Therapy. Disease: Iron Deficiency Anemia. title: Botulism: Clostridium botulinum Neurotoxin and Descending Flaccid Paralysis
chunk_text: Botulism: Clostridium botulinum Neurotoxin and Descending Flaccid Paralysis. Disease: Botulism. Botulism is a rare but life-threatening neuroparalytic syndrome caused by botulinum neurotoxins—the most potent biological toxins known. The toxin irreversibly cleaves SNARE proteins at presynaptic cholinergic neuromuscular junctions, blocking acetylcholine release. Prompt clinical diagnosis without waiting for laboratory bioassay results is imperative because antitoxin only halts progression by neutralizing circulating, unbound neurotoxin.

Nephrotic syndrome is a classic clinical triad characterized by nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 grams per 24 hours per 1.73 m²), hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL), and generalized edema, accompanied by hyperlipidemia and lipiduria (oval fat bodies exhibiting 'Maltese cross' appearance under polarized light). Urinary loss of antithrombin III and plasminogen leads to a hypercoagulable state with elevated risk of deep vein thrombosis and renal vein thrombosis. Renal biopsy with light, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy is the definitive diagnostic standard in adults.

title: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD): Cystogenesis and Tolvaptan
chunk_text: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD): Cystogenesis and Tolvaptan. Disease: Polycystic Kidney Disease. Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic cause of kidney failure. Mutations lead to dysregulated tubular epithelial cell proliferation and continuous fluid secretion, generating countless expanding fluid-filled cysts that progressively destroy functioning renal parenchyma over decades. Extrarenal manifestations include hepatic cysts (polycystic liver), pancreatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula, and intracranial berry aneurysms of the circle of Willis, which carry risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage.

chunk_text: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD): Cystogenesis and Tolvaptan (Polycystic Kidney Disease). chunk_text: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD / NAFLD): Steatohepatitis and Fibrosis. Disease: Fatty Liver Disease. title: Liver Cirrhosis: Portal Hypertension, Ascites, and Hepatic Encephalopathy
chunk_text: Liver Cirrhosis: Portal Hypertension, Ascites, and Hepatic Encephalopathy. Disease: Cirrhosis. Liver cirrhosis is characterized by diffuse architectural distortion with regenerative parenchymal nodules surrounded by dense fibrous septa. Fibrosis increases intrahepatic vascular resistance, generating portal hypertension (hepatic venous pressure gradient >=10 mmHg). Critical decompensations include bleeding gastroesophageal varices, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), hepatorenal syndrome, and hepatic encephalopathy resulting from impaired clearance of gut-derived neurotoxins such as ammonia. The Child-Pugh and MELD-Na scores quantify liver disease severity.

title: Viral Hepatitis B: Chronic Infection, Serological Markers, and Nucleoside Analogs
chunk_text: Viral Hepatitis B: Chronic Infection, Serological Markers, and Nucleoside Analogs. Disease: Hepatitis B. Hepatitis B virus infection is a major cause of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and primary liver cancer worldwide. Diagnosis relies on serological panels: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) indicates active infection; anti-HBs indicates immunity; anti-HBc IgM signifies acute infection; HBeAg denotes high viral replication and infectivity. Progression to chronicity occurs in >90% of perinatally infected infants but only ~5% of immunocompetent adults. Long-term antiviral therapy suppresses serum HBV DNA and reduces cirrhosis progression.

title: Viral Hepatitis C: Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) and Sustained Virologic Response
chunk_text: Viral Hepatitis C: Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) and Sustained Virologic Response. Disease: Hepatitis C. Hepatitis C virus causes both acute and chronic hepatitis, with chronicity developing in 70-85% of untreated individuals. Historically treated with poorly tolerated interferon-based regimens, HCV management underwent a revolution with the advent of direct-acting antivirals targeting viral NS3/4A protease, NS5A replication complex, and NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Achieving a sustained virologic response (undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment, SVR12) equates to a virological cure and dramatically reduces future cirrhosis and mortality.

chunk_text: Allergic Rhinitis: IgE-Mediated Type I Hypersensitivity and Intranasal Corticosteroids. Disease: Allergic Rhinitis. Allergic rhinitis is an extremely common inflammatory disorder of the nasal mucosa provoked by allergen exposure. Upon contact with sensitized nasal mucosa, cross-linking of surface-bound IgE molecules triggers immediate mast cell degranulation, releasing preformed mediators including histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins that cause immediate pruritus and vasodilatation. A late-phase reaction develops 4 to 8 hours later, driven by eosinophil and T-lymphocyte infiltration causing prolonged nasal blockage.

title: Anaphylaxis: Systemic IgE-Mediated Degranulation and Intramuscular Epinephrine Protocol
chunk_text: Anaphylaxis: Systemic IgE-Mediated Degranulation and Intramuscular Epinephrine Protocol. Disease: Anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is an acute, severe, potentially fatal multi-system hypersensitivity reaction that can develop within seconds to minutes of allergen exposure. Epinephrine is the only definitive life-saving medication; it acts on alpha-1 receptors to reverse peripheral vasodilatation and reduce mucosal edema, beta-1 receptors to increase cardiac contractility, and beta-2 receptors to produce bronchodilation and attenuate further mediator release. Delaying epinephrine administration is the primary contributor to fatal anaphylactic outcomes.

title: Crohn's Disease: Transmural Granulomatous Ileocolitis and Biologic Anti-TNF Therapy
chunk_text: Crohn's Disease: Transmural Granulomatous Ileocolitis and Biologic Anti-TNF Therapy. Disease: Crohn's Disease. Crohn's disease is an idiopathic chronic inflammatory bowel disease capable of affecting any segment of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus, with a predilection for the terminal ileum and cecum ('terminal ileitis'). Colonoscopy classically demonstrates discontinuous mucosal involvement ('skip lesions'), cobblestone mucosal appearance, and deep linear ulcerations. Histopathology reveals transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. Complications include mechanical bowel obstruction from fibrostenotic strictures, enteroenteric fistulae, and intra-abdominal abscesses.

chunk_text: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Gut-Brain Axis, Rome IV Criteria, and Low-FODMAP Diet. Disease: Irritable Bowel Syndrome. Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder diagnosed via the Rome IV criteria: recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, associated with two or more of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, or change in stool form. Subtypes include IBS with predominant constipation (IBS-C), IBS with predominant diarrhea (IBS-D), mixed (IBS-M), and unclassified. Diagnosis requires absence of red flag 'alarm features' (unintentional weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, rectal bleeding, onset after age 50, anemia, family history of colorectal cancer).

source: American College of Gastroenterology & NIH MedlinePlus
chunk_text: Acute Pancreatitis: Gallstones, Alcohol, Lipase Elevation, and Atlanta Classification. Disease: Acute Pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis involves acute non-bacterial enzymatic autodigestion of the pancreatic parenchyma triggered by premature intracellular activation of trypsinogen to trypsin within acinar cells. Diagnosis requires at least two of three criteria: typical severe epigastric abdominal pain, serum amylase or lipase elevated >=3 times upper limit of normal, and characteristic cross-sectional imaging findings (contrast-enhanced CT or MRI). The revised Atlanta classification stratifies severity into mild (no organ failure), moderately severe (transient organ failure <48 hours), and severe (persistent organ failure >48 hours).

chunk_text: Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Meningococcal and Pneumococcal Central Nervous System Infection. Disease: Bacterial Meningitis. Acute bacterial meningitis is a life-threatening medical emergency requiring urgent diagnosis and treatment within minutes. Bacterial lysis in the subarachnoid space triggers intense neutrophil infiltration, cerebral edema, heightened intracranial pressure, and decreased cerebral perfusion. Lumbar puncture reveals purulent CSF under elevated opening pressure, elevated polymorphonuclear pleocytosis (>1000/mm³), high protein (>100 mg/dL), and markedly depressed CSF-to-serum glucose ratio (<0.4). Delay in antibiotic administration significantly increases mortality and long-term neurosensory hearing loss.

title: Acute Pericarditis: Pericardial Friction Rub, PR Depression, and Colchicine
source: European Society of Cardiology & NIH MedlinePlus
chunk_text: Acute Pericarditis: Pericardial Friction Rub, PR Depression, and Colchicine. Disease: Pericarditis. Acute pericarditis is an inflammatory disorder of the pericardial sac surrounding the heart. Diagnostic criteria require at least two of the following: characteristic positional pleuritic chest pain; auscultatory pericardial friction rub; widespread concavity-upward ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression on 12-lead ECG; and new or worsening pericardial effusion on echocardiography. The major acute complication is cardiac tamponade, wherein fluid accumulation produces elevated intrapericardial pressure, jugular venous distension, hypotension, and pulsus paradoxus.

chunk_text: Acute Pericarditis: Pericardial Friction Rub, PR Depression, and Colchicine (Pericarditis). title: Deep Vein Thrombosis: Lower Extremity Thrombus, D-dimer, and Compression Ultrasonography
chunk_text: Deep Vein Thrombosis: Lower Extremity Thrombus, D-dimer, and Compression Ultrasonography. Disease: Deep Vein Thrombosis. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) represents the venous phase of venous thromboembolism. Without timely therapeutic intervention, fragments of lower extremity thrombi frequently detach and embolize through the inferior vena cava and right cardiac chambers to occlude the pulmonary circulation, causing potentially fatal pulmonary embolism. Compression duplex ultrasonography of the lower extremity veins—evaluating lack of venous luminal compressibility under probe pressure—is the primary diagnostic gold standard.

chunk_text: Multiple Sclerosis: Central Nervous System Demyelination, Oligoclonal Bands, and Disease-Modifying Therapies. Disease: Multiple Sclerosis. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the premier non-traumatic disabling neurological disease affecting young adults, typically diagnosed between ages 20 and 40. Clinical patterns include relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS, ~85% of cases), primary progressive MS (PPMS), and secondary progressive MS (SPMS). The McDonald criteria define diagnosis by establishing dissemination of inflammatory white-matter demyelinating lesions in both space and time on gadolinium-enhanced brain and spinal cord MRI, supported by detection of cerebrospinal fluid-restricted oligoclonal IgG bands.

source: American Academy of Otolaryngology & Mayo Clinic
chunk_text: Bell's Palsy: Idiopathic Peripheral Facial Nerve Paralysis and Corticosteroid Therapy. Disease: Bell's Palsy. Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral peripheral facial nerve neuropathy. A key clinical hallmark distinguishing Bell's palsy (lower motor neuron lesion) from central ischemic stroke (upper motor neuron lesion) is involvement of the forehead muscles: in Bell's palsy, forehead wrinkling and eye closure are paralyzed on the affected side due to denervation, whereas in stroke, bilateral cortical innervation spares forehead movement. Over 70-80% of patients recover complete facial motor function spontaneously within 3 to 6 months.

chunk_text: Typhoid Fever: Salmonella Typhi Bacteremia, Widal Reaction, and Fluoroquinolone Resistance. Disease: Typhoid Fever. Typhoid (enteric) fever is an invasive bacterial infection endemic in regions with deficient water and sanitation infrastructure. Ingested bacilli invade the intestinal mucosa via M cells of Peyer's patches, where they survive intracellularly within mononuclear phagocytes and disseminate into the bloodstream and reticuloendothelial system. Without targeted antibiotic therapy, severe complications arise in the 3rd and 4th weeks: intestinal perforation of ulcerated Peyer's patches and massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Blood culture remains the diagnostic gold standard, outperforming unreliable Widal serology.

Symptoms and Signs: Gradual, painless, progressive blurriness of vision, dulling or yellowing of color perception, glare and halos around headlights during night driving, poor night vision, frequent changes in eyeglass prescriptions ('second sight'). Causes and Etiology: Aggregation and oxidation of crystalline lens structural proteins (crystallins) secondary to aging, ultraviolet radiation exposure, smoking, diabetes mellitus, systemic corticosteroid therapy, or ocular trauma.

title: Cataracts: Crystalline Lens Opacification, Phacoemulsification, and Intraocular Lenses
chunk_text: Cataracts: Crystalline Lens Opacification, Phacoemulsification, and Intraocular Lenses (Cataracts). Treatment and Clinical Management: Definitive curative management is ambulatory surgical extraction via modern phacoemulsification (ultrasonic fragmentation of the opaque lens) followed by implantation of a biocompatible synthetic intraocular lens (monofocal, multifocal, or toric IOL). Prevention and Lifestyle Recommendations: Wearing sunglasses blocking 100% of UVA and UVB radiation, smoking cessation, maintaining tight glycemic control in diabetics, consuming antioxidant-rich diets, and avoiding unnecessary prolonged systemic or topical ophthalmic steroids.

title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Antinuclear Antibodies, Immune Complex Vasculitis, and Hydroxychloroquine
source: American College of Rheumatology & NIH MedlinePlus
chunk_text: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Antinuclear Antibodies, Immune Complex Vasculitis, and Hydroxychloroquine. Disease: Lupus. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a prototypical multi-system autoimmune disorder predominantly affecting women of childbearing age. Immune complex deposition activates the classical complement pathway, resulting in hypocomplementemia (low C3 and C4) and widespread inflammatory tissue injury. Lupus nephritis is a major determinant of overall morbidity and mortality, requiring surveillance with routine urinalysis, protein-to-creatinine ratio, and renal biopsy. Antiphospholipid syndrome co-occurs in ~30% of patients, heightening vascular thrombosis and pregnancy loss risks.

chunk_text: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Antinuclear Antibodies, Immune Complex Vasculitis, and Hydroxychloroquine (Lupus). Symptoms and Signs: Malar 'butterfly' rash sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, discoid skin lesions, non-erosive polyarthritis, oral ulcers, serositis (pleurisy, pericarditis), lupus nephritis (proteinuria, cellular casts), autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia. Causes and Etiology: Systemic autoimmune disease driven by defective clearance of apoptotic material, generation of autoantibodies against nuclear antigens (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith), and systemic immune-complex deposition in microvasculature.

source: American College of Rheumatology & NIH MedlinePlus
chunk_text: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Antinuclear Antibodies, Immune Complex Vasculitis, and Hydroxychloroquine (Lupus). Treatment and Clinical Management: Universal baseline therapy with hydroxychloroquine for all patients to prevent flares and organ damage; systemic corticosteroids for acute exacerbations; immunosuppressants (mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine); targeted B-cell biologics (belimumab, anifrolumab). Prevention and Lifestyle Recommendations: Strict photoprotection (broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing) to prevent UV-induced apoptosis and disease flares, smoking cessation, and adherence to maintenance hydroxychloroquine.

title: Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa: Eating Disorders, Medical Complications, and Refeeding Syndrome
source: American Psychiatric Association & National Eating Disorders Association
chunk_text: Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa: Eating Disorders, Medical Complications, and Refeeding Syndrome. Disease: Eating Disorders. Eating disorders are severe psychiatric illnesses carrying profound medical complications. Severe malnutrition in anorexia nervosa causes sinus bradycardia, orthostatic hypotension, amenorrhea, leukopenia, and osteoporosis. Rapid reintroduction of carbohydrates in severely malnourished patients triggers refeeding syndrome—characterized by fatal hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and cardiac arrhythmias resulting from sudden insulin-mediated intracellular ion shifting. Close electrolyte monitoring is mandatory during early refeeding.

title: Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa: Eating Disorders, Medical Complications, and Refeeding Syndrome
source: American Psychiatric Association & National Eating Disorders Association
chunk_text: Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa: Eating Disorders, Medical Complications, and Refeeding Syndrome (Eating Disorders). Symptoms and Signs: Severe restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, distorted body image (anorexia); recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory purging behaviors (bulimia); Russell sign (calluses on knuckles), parotid gland hypertrophy, enamel erosion. Causes and Etiology: Complex multifactorial etiologies involving neurobiological alterations in serotonin and dopamine reward pathways, genetic vulnerabilities, perfectionistic personality traits, and sociocultural pressures valorizing thinness.

title: Measles (Rubeola): Paramyxovirus Transmission, Koplik Spots, and MMR Vaccination
chunk_text: Measles (Rubeola): Paramyxovirus Transmission, Koplik Spots, and MMR Vaccination. Disease: Measles. Measles is one of the most contagious human pathogens known. Following viral replication within the respiratory epithelium and draining lymph nodes, widespread viremia causes profound temporary immune suppression ('immune amnesia') that leaves patients highly susceptible to secondary bacterial infections for months. Major complications include severe pneumonia (the leading cause of measles death in children), acute encephalitis, corneal ulceration, and a fatal late neurodegenerative sequela occurring years later termed subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE).

title: Measles (Rubeola): Paramyxovirus Transmission, Koplik Spots, and MMR Vaccination
chunk_text: Measles (Rubeola): Paramyxovirus Transmission, Koplik Spots, and MMR Vaccination (Measles). Symptoms and Signs: High fever, the classic '3 Cs' (cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis), Koplik spots (small bluish-white spots on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa), followed by an erythematous maculopapular rash spreading cephalocaudally from hairline to trunk and extremities. Causes and Etiology: Measles virus, an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Morbillivirus (family Paramyxoviridae), transmitted via aerosolized respiratory droplets with extreme contagiousness (R0 of 12-18).

chunk_text: Measles (Rubeola): Paramyxovirus Transmission, Koplik Spots, and MMR Vaccination (Measles). Treatment and Clinical Management: Supportive management: antipyretics, hydration; high-dose oral Vitamin A supplementation administered on two consecutive days to reduce blindness and pneumonia mortality; airborne infection isolation precautions. Prevention and Lifestyle Recommendations: Two doses of the live attenuated Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) vaccine (first dose at 12-15 months, second dose at 4-6 years), conferring over 97% lifelong immunity and establishing robust herd protection when population coverage exceeds 95%.

title: Biliary Colic and Acute Cholecystitis: Gallstone Obstruction, Murphy's Sign, and Cholecystectomy
source: Tokyo Guidelines & American College of Gastroenterology
chunk_text: Biliary Colic and Acute Cholecystitis: Gallstone Obstruction, Murphy's Sign, and Cholecystectomy. Disease: Cholecystitis. Acute cholecystitis is an inflammatory infection of the gallbladder wall predominantly arising as a complication of cholelithiasis. In contrast to transient biliary colic, the pain of acute cholecystitis persists for more than 6 hours and is accompanied by systemic inflammatory markers. Abdominal ultrasound is the primary initial imaging procedure of choice, revealing gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening (>4 mm), pericholecystic fluid, and a sonographic Murphy sign. Untreated cases risk gangrenous necrosis, gallbladder perforation, and peritonitis.

chunk_text: Biliary Colic and Acute Cholecystitis: Gallstone Obstruction, Murphy's Sign, and Cholecystectomy (Cholecystitis). Symptoms and Signs: Severe constant right upper quadrant (RUQ) or epigastric pain radiating to the right shoulder or back, lasting >4-6 hours, accompanied by fever, leukocytosis, nausea, vomiting, and positive Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation of RUQ). Causes and Etiology: Sustained cystic duct obstruction by an impacted gallstone (calculous cholecystitis in ~95% of cases), causing mechanical gallbladder distention, mucosal ischemia, chemical irritation by lysolecithin, and secondary bacterial infection.

chunk_text: Biliary Colic and Acute Cholecystitis: Gallstone Obstruction, Murphy's Sign, and Cholecystectomy (Cholecystitis). Treatment and Clinical Management: Inpatient admission, bowel rest (NPO), intravenous fluid resuscitation, multimodal parenteral analgesia, empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone plus metronidazole); early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 24-72 hours of admission. title: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Dysregulated Host Response, qSOFA Criteria, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign
chunk_text: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Dysregulated Host Response, qSOFA Criteria, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign. Disease: Sepsis. Sepsis is a major global healthcare crisis accounting for approximately 20% of all global deaths. The Sepsis-3 consensus definition defines sepsis as an acute change in total Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score >=2 points consequent to infection. Septic shock represents a subset where underlying circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities are profound enough to substantially increase mortality, identified by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >=65 mmHg and serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

title: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Dysregulated Host Response, qSOFA Criteria, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign
chunk_text: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Dysregulated Host Response, qSOFA Criteria, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign (Sepsis). Symptoms and Signs: Hypothermia (<36°C) or hyperthermia (>38.3°C), severe tachycardia (>90 bpm), tachypnea (>20 bpm), acute confusion or encephalopathy, extreme shivering or muscle pain, mottled cold skin, oliguria, hypotension unresponsive to initial fluid resuscitation. Causes and Etiology: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated systemic host response to an infection (pneumonia, UTI, intra-abdominal sepsis, skin/soft tissue infection), triggering widespread endothelial injury, capillary leak, and microvascular thrombosis.

title: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Dysregulated Host Response, qSOFA Criteria, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign
chunk_text: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Dysregulated Host Response, qSOFA Criteria, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign (Sepsis). Treatment and Clinical Management: The 'Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle': measure blood lactate level; obtain blood cultures prior to antibiotics; administer empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antimicrobials; rapid infusion of 30 mL/kg crystalloids for hypotension or lactate >=4 mmol/L; administer vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line) to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) >=65 mmHg. Prevention and Lifestyle Recommendations: Preventing infections through vaccination (influenza, pneumococcus), sterile surgical and catheter techniques in hospitals, prompt treatment of localized infections (UTIs, cellulitis, pneumonia), and good community hygiene.
